paper_context.research_question: Can a minimalist neural approach that uses a dependency-guided localized context window (Predicate Window / PreWin) plus modest training data match or exceed prior metonymy resolution performance while requiring fewer external resources, and can a newly annotated Wikipedia-based dataset (ReLocaR) improve training and evaluation for location metonymy?
contribution_style: experimental comparison to baselines and prior SOTA
main_claims: Predicate Window (PreWin), a dependency-head-guided local context extractor, plus a small LSTM-based model, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the SemEval 2007 metonymy resolution task (location subset) while using far fewer external resources than prior systems.
PreWin outperforms common baselines (immediate left/right windows and paragraph-level context) with smaller input sizes and higher discriminative power.
An ensemble of models (trained on combinations of SemEval, ReLocaR, and an annotated CoNLL subset) further improves performance, matching or slightly exceeding previous SOTA.

ReLocaR, a new Wikipedia-derived dataset with revised annotation guidelines (notably treating political/government senses as metonymic), provides a less-biased class distribution and useful additional training data for MR.

The minimalist approach generalises sufficiently within datasets (good accuracy on ReLocaR and SemEval individually) but shows limited cross-dataset transfer, plausibly due to differences in annotation schemes.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: classification accuracy and class-wise F1 (literal vs non-literal) on standard test sets (SemEval 2007, ReLocaR)
statistical significance of improvements over baselines and prior work (noting dataset size limits)
comparison of PreWin to immediate-window and paragraph baselines in terms of input size vs performance trade-offs
robustness to parser errors and sensitivity to dependency parsing choices
ablation: effect of PreWin window size, inclusion/exclusion of entity tokens, embedding dimensionality, and LSTM architecture choices
cross-dataset generalisation (train on one dataset, test on another) to assess annotation/transfer sensitivity
annotation quality and inter-annotator agreement for ReLocaR (IAA reported) and documentation of revised guidelines
resource availability and reproducibility (release of ReLocaR, annotated CoNLL subset, code/models)

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: A single local dependency-head-directed window of up to 5 words contains sufficient disambiguating context for most metonymy resolution cases.

Section 5.2: claim that 'Most of the time (typically 85% for the two datasets), PreWin is sufficient for an accurate classification.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If important disambiguating cues frequently lie outside the 5-word predicate window, the method will systematically miss signals, reducing accuracy and biasing error patterns; ensemble or larger-window baselines may be preferable.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Dependency head links reliably point toward predicates that are informative for metonymy resolution when using SpaCy parser.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.1: PreWin follows the entity head dependency to point to predicate.
Section 5.3: parser mistakes noted as infrequent but consequential.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the parser frequently selects non-informative heads or misparses structures, PreWin will extract irrelevant context leading to misclassification; results may not generalise to other parsers or genres.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Excluding the entity token itself from model input does not remove essential lexical cues needed for classification.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.1: explicit statement that entity token is never used as input and model relies on context.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the entity lexical form provides crucial disambiguating information (e.g., orthographic cues, known entity-specific senses), excluding it could lower performance, especially on rare contexts or when context is noisy.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: GloVe 50-dimensional pre-trained embeddings initialized on the limited vocabulary are appropriate and sufficient for this task and dataset sizes.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2: use of top 100k GloVe vectors and 50-dim as default.

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the chosen embeddings inadequately capture relevant senses or domain vocabulary, model may underperform; reported advantage for 50-dim may be dataset-specific and not generalise.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The revised annotation guideline (treating government/political senses as metonymic) yields a more useful or less biased dataset for MR and explains cross-dataset differences.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that a narrowly targeted dependency-head-guided context extractor (Predicate Window, PreWin) combined with a small LSTM-based classifier can match or slightly exceed prior SOTA on location metonymy resolution while using far fewer external resources. It also introduces ReLocaR, a Wikipedia-derived dataset with revised annotation guidelines (notably treating governmental/political senses as metonymic) and an annotated CoNLL subset as auxiliary data. Empirical evidence is presented via comparisons to immediate-window and paragraph baselines and previous SOTA numbers on SemEval 2007, plus internal evaluation on ReLocaR and cross-dataset transfer experiments. The logical chain links a linguistic intuition (most disambiguating cues are in a small predicate-focused window) to a concrete extraction method (PreWin), to a modest neural model, to empirical gains. Strengths include a clear feature-design rationale, focused ablations versus simple baselines, and a new dataset with IAA reported for the test partition. Weaknesses in the argumentative chain are: incomplete reporting of experimental variance and hyperparameters, under-specified dataset sampling/adjudication procedures, single-annotator training resources (CoNLL subset), limited analysis of parser sensitivity, and the marginal magnitude/significance of the claimed SOTA. Several assumptions (e.g., that excluding the entity token is safe, that 5-word PreWin captures required context) are plausible but not fully isolated by ablations. Overall the paper presents a coherent, mostly consistent argument with concrete empirical support but leaves important verification steps under-specified; follow-up experiments (multiple random seeds, parser-variation, ablations including the entity token, and resampling diagnostics for ReLocaR) are necessary to solidify the claims.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes Predicate Window (PreWin), a dependency-head-directed local context extractor, combined with a compact LSTM-based architecture and modest training data, to perform location metonymy resolution. It introduces ReLocaR, a Wikipedia-derived dataset with revised annotation guidelines (treating political/government senses as metonymic) and an annotated CoNLL subset. Empirically, single PreWin models reach competitive accuracy on SemEval 2007 and ReLocaR; small ensembles slightly improve these numbers and marginally exceed the previous SemEval SOTA. The paper emphasizes minimal external resources and argues that dependency-guided, small windows provide better signal-to-noise trade-offs than immediate (fixed) windows or paragraph-level context. Key methodological claims rest on (a) PreWin reliably locating disambiguating predicates using SpaCy parses, (b) excluding the entity token from input is acceptable, (c) 5-word windows are generally sufficient, and (d) ReLocaR's revised guidelines produce a less-biased dataset. Reporting lacks many reproducibility details (seeds, full hyperparameters, exact preprocessing and ensemble mechanics), limited ablations (no quantified entity-inclusion ablation, sparse parser-sensitivity experiments), and partial release/access statements (CoNLL subset available only on request). Statistical claims are mixed: authors admit the SemEval SOTA margin is not significant at 95%, yet claim very high significance for PreWin vs baselines without full methodology and variance reporting. Cross-dataset transfer drops are observed but not isolated between annotation-scheme effects, parser/genre differences, or sampling biases.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Most disambiguating context for location metonymy can be found in a local predicate-oriented window pointed to by the entity's dependency head.
A2: SpaCy dependency parsing reliably identifies the head from which PreWin extracts up to 5 context words and dependency labels.
A3: The LSTM architecture (4 LSTMs: left/right words and left/right dependency labels) with 50-dim GloVe embeddings effectively models the PreWin outputs.
A4: Excluding the entity token does not remove essential lexical cues; context suffices.
A5: PreWin reduces input noise versus immediate/paragraph baselines, improving discriminative power and requiring fewer external resources.
A6: ReLocaR's sampling and revised annotation (government->metonymic) yield a balanced dataset useful for training and explain cross-dataset transfer drops.
A7: Ensembles of modest models trained on different data/configurations combine complementary strengths to slightly exceed prior SOTA.

Consequences: If A1-A4 hold, PreWin will outperform naively sized windows with less data and fewer resources; if any fail (parser errors, entity lexical cues, long-range dependencies), performance drops and transferability suffers.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that metonymy resolution (MR) for location mentions can be achieved competitively using a narrowly focused, dependency-head-guided local context extractor (Predicate Window, PreWin) plus a lightweight LSTM architecture and modest training data. The reasoning is: (1) many prior MR systems rely on large external resources, broad context windows, or heavy feature engineering; (2) linguistic intuition and parser-guided selection identify a small predicate-proximal region that often contains the decisive cue for whether a location is used metonymically; (3) extracting up to 5 words starting at the entity head dependency (skipping punctuation/conj) yields a compact input that reduces noise; (4) feeding this input (and dependency labels) into a small LSTM model (with pretrained GloVe embeddings) can match or slightly exceed prior SOTA on SemEval 2007 (location subset) and perform well on a new balanced Wikipedia-derived dataset (ReLocaR); (5) ensembling models trained on different corpora yields small further gains; (6) annotation guideline changes (treating government/political senses as metonymic) and a new dataset help address training bias and distributional imbalance. The authors support these claims with comparative tables (PreWin vs immediate/paragraph baselines, single models vs ensembles), IAA on ReLocaR test subset, and qualitative error analysis pointing to parser limits and rare semantic patterns. Key methodological gaps include limited reporting of variance across runs, incomplete ablations (e.g., inclusion of entity token), and under-specified dataset sampling/adjudication details. Overall, the contribution is an incremental but focused methodological refinement (a dependency-directed local window) combined with a dataset/resource offering; its novelty lies in the particular operationalisation (PreWin + exclusion of entity token) and the empirical claim that small, discriminative context plus modest models can replace heavier-resource systems for this MR subtask.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: metonymy undermines NER/GP; prior MR systems use many external resources and broad context windows.
Observation: disambiguating cues are often local but not necessarily in immediate adjacent tokens; dependency heads point to predicates that carry semantic selectional information.
Design choice: define PreWin as up-to-5-word window starting at the entity's dependency head, skipping punctuation and conjunctions; do not include the entity token itself.
Model: process PreWin words + dependency labels with four LSTMs and pretrained GloVe(50d); prefer LSTM over MLP/CNN based on earlier (briefly reported) comparisons.
Datasets: create ReLocaR (balanced Wikipedia sample, revised guideline treating government senses as metonymic) and annotate CoNLL subset for auxiliary training.
Experiments: compare PreWin vs immediate(5/10) and paragraph baselines on SemEval and ReLocaR; run ensembles combining models trained on different corpora/configs.

Results: single PreWin models approach or match prior SOTA numerically on SemEval (85.0 vs 86.2 SOTA single-model numbers) and achieve high scores on ReLocaR (84.3); ensembles slightly exceed prior SOTA numerically (86.3 vs 86.2).
Analysis: attribute modest cross-dataset transfer drops to annotation differences and parsing/genre variations; note limitations (parser sensitivity, rare constructions).

Conclusion: a highly discriminative, dependency-guided local context plus compact neural architecture can be an effective, resource-efficient approach to location MR; ReLocaR addresses prior dataset bias and is a useful resource.

alternative_interpretations: The reported gains over baselines stem primarily from better preprocessing or parser configurations rather than the conceptual novelty of PreWin; slight differences in tokenisation/parse decisions could change which words are included in the window.

If PreWin's 5-word window matches the majority of linguistic patterns where predicates host selectional cues, the method will remain robust; otherwise performance will degrade on sentences with distributed cues.

If datasets and annotation schemes align (or the guideline change is isolated and quantified), training on combined corpora will produce stable improvements rather than artefactual gains from label distributions.
If alternative parsers and padding/masking strategies are used and results remain stable, the method's robustness to implementation choices will be demonstrated.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Reconstruction of the paper's reasoning chain: The authors begin with the premise that metonymy resolution (MR) is primarily driven by local predicate/context, not by the entity surface form or large paragraph context. From corpus inspection and prior dependency-based approaches, they propose Predicate Window (PreWin): follow the entity's dependency head to extract up to five tokens (skipping punctuation and conjunctions) and their dependency labels, forming a compact, dependency-guided context. They pair this extractor with a small neural classifier (four LSTMs encoding left/right tokens and left/right dependency-label sequences), initialize with 50-dim GloVe embeddings, and explicitly exclude the entity token from inputs to force reliance on context. Empirically, they train/test on SemEval 2007 (locations), introduce ReLocaR (Wikipedia-derived, balanced classes, revised guideline treating government-as-metonymy), and an annotated CoNLL subset as auxiliary data. Results show (1) PreWin single models beat immediate (5/10) and paragraph baselines with smaller input budgets, (2) ensembles across data/configs yield marginally higher accuracy (ensemble SemEval 86.3% vs prior 86.2%), and (3) ReLocaR single/ensemble results are comparable to SemEval. The authors acknowledge limitations: small dataset sizes, marginal SOTA gains not significant at 95% for SemEval, parser-dependence (SpaCy), sampling/balancing choices for ReLocaR, and missing full ablation/variance reporting. Their central claim is that a linguistically informed, dependency-head-localized window plus a modest neural model can recover or slightly exceed prior MR performance while using far fewer external resources.
logical_argument_graph: Observation: Most words in sentence/paragraph are often irrelevant for MR -> motivates focusing on minimal context
Linguistic intuition: predicate linked by entity's dependency head is often the decisive cue -> design: PreWin extracts tokens from head outward
Design decision: limit to 5 tokens to trade off precision/recall and avoid noise -> operationalize as predicate window
Modeling choice: exclude entity token to force context-based decisions -> small LSTM architecture encodes PreWin (tokens + labels)
Experiment: train on SemEval/ReLocaR/CoNLL subsets -> measure accuracy and per-class F1
Result: PreWin > immediate/paragraph baselines on both datasets -> claim: PreWin is more discriminating with less input
Result: Ensemble models (different data/embeddings/architectures) yield small extra gains -> claim: ensemble attains marginal SOTA
Dataset work: ReLocaR created with balanced classes and revised annotation (government-as-metonymy) -> claim: better class balance and clearer guidelines
Observed limitation: cross-dataset transfer degrades significantly -> hypothesis: annotation-guideline differences (and parser/genre) drive transfer failure
Conclusion: Minimalist dependency-guided windows are a viable, resource-light alternative to heavy feature engineering / external KBs, but need further validation across parsers/datasets

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes Predicate Window (PreWin), a dependency-head-guided local context extractor combined with a compact LSTM-based classifier, and introduces ReLocaR, a Wikipedia-derived dataset with revised annotation guidelines. The authors argue that PreWin—by extracting up to five tokens outward from the entity head (skipping punctuation/conjunctions) and excluding the entity token itself—yields more discriminative, smaller inputs than immediate fixed windows or paragraph contexts and thus can match or slightly exceed prior SOTA on the SemEval 2007 location metonymy task while using fewer external resources. Empirical results show PreWin single-model accuracy 85.0% (SemEval coarse) and ensemble 86.3% (compared to prior 86.2), ReLocaR single-model 84.3% and ensemble 85.7%. ReLocaR (1k train / 1k test) is claimed to have balanced classes (49/49/2) and high IAA on test slices. The paper provides qualitative error analysis pointing to parser and semantic-complexity failure modes. Evidence in the manuscript supports that PreWin outperforms the implemented immediate/paragraph baselines on presented datasets and that ReLocaR has different annotation choices (political/government senses marked metonymic) that plausibly explain cross-dataset drops. However, several evidentiary gaps remain: variance across runs and full statistical testing details are missing; important ablations (including entity token, padding effects, parser variation, full window-size sweep) are not reported; the CoNLL auxiliary set lacks IAA; ReLocaR sampling/balancing procedures and full release metadata are under-specified. Where claims are narrowly scoped to the reported experimental setup, manuscript evidence supports them; when claims are generalized (robust cross-dataset generalisation, parser-independence, SOTA superiority writ large), they are partially supported or overstated given the provided evidence and admitted marginal significance.
logical_argument_graph: Linguistic intuition: disambiguating cues for metonymy are often in a small predicate-centered region rather than uniformly in a fixed local window or whole paragraph.
Operationalization: use dependency parser (SpaCy) to find entity head and extract up to 5 tokens outward (PreWin), skip punctuation/conj, exclude entity token from input.
Modeling: feed PreWin tokens + dependency labels into a compact four-LSTM architecture with pretrained GloVe (50d) embeddings.
Empirical test: train/test on SemEval and new ReLocaR, compare PreWin vs immediate windows (5/10) and paragraph baseline; evaluate ensembles combining models trained on different corpora/configs.

Observed results: PreWin single-model outperforms immediate/paragraph baselines on both datasets; ensembles gain small additional improvements; cross-dataset transfer drops when training/testing across SemEval/ReLocaR.

Interpretation: focused dependency-guided windows reduce noise and achieve strong signal-to-noise tradeoff; annotation differences (government=metonymic in ReLocaR) and parser choices likely drive transfer limits.

Limitations: admitted marginal SOTA improvement (not significant at 95% for SemEval overall), absence of detailed variance reporting, limited ablations, under-specified dataset sampling & some single-annotator resources.

consensus_findings: PreWin (dependency-head-guided predicate window) is a coherent, linguistically motivated extractor that yields compact, higher-signal inputs compared to immediate fixed windows and paragraph-level context in the reported experiments.

On the reported experimental setup (SpaCy parsing, GloVe(50d), single-training runs reported), PreWin single models consistently outperform the implemented Immediate5/Immediate10 and Paragraph baselines on both SemEval and ReLocaR.

ReLocaR is a new Wikipedia-derived dataset (1,000 train / 1,000 test) created to reduce class imbalance; the authors report test-partition IAA figures for annotated subsets and explicitly document a guideline difference (treating governmental/political senses as metonymic).

Ensembling models trained on different data/configurations produces small additional gains and in the authors' configuration reaches parity or slight numerical improvement relative to a previously reported SemEval number.

The manuscript acknowledges key limitations: parser dependence (SpaCy), marginal magnitude of SOTA-level improvement, and several under-specified methodological details (hyperparameters, seeds, ablations, sampling scripts).
disagreements: Extent of novelty: some reviewers view PreWin as an incremental operational refinement (dependency-path ideas are antecedent), while others treat the specific combination (head-directed window + entity-exclusion + compact LSTM) as a noteworthy innovation absent in prior MR literature.

Interpretation of ensemble SOTA parity: reviewers agree the ensemble numerically matches/exceeds a prior reported number by a tiny margin, but disagree whether that constitutes a substantive advance given the ensemble uses auxiliary annotated data (CoNLL subset) and the improvement is not robustly significant at conventional thresholds.

Sufficiency of current evidence: some reviewers are moderately confident that PreWin's gains are real and practically useful even without additional experiments, whereas others judge missing ablations, multi-run variance, parser-sensitivity tests, and dataset-sampling transparency as critical gaps that materially reduce confidence in generalisability.

Risk posed by single-annotator CoNLL auxiliary data: reviewers differ on how much this undermines ensemble claims—some see it as a manageable caveat (request-access resource), others call it a major methodological concern requiring IAA/spot-checks before treating ensemble results as reliable.
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical robustness: no reported means/std across multiple random seeds or full description of statistical tests; the SOTA margin is numerically marginal and some claimed contrasts lack reproducible p-value methodology.

Ablation gaps: critical design choices lack controlled tests (include vs exclude entity token; PreWin window-size sweep; dependency-label ablation; padding/masking strategy), leaving causal attribution of gains uncertain.
Parser sensitivity: dependence on SpaCy for head selection is acknowledged but not quantified; sensitivity to alternative parsers or parsing error rates is untested.

ReLocaR sampling and balancing: the procedure for discarding excess literal examples is under-specified, creating risk of sampling bias that could affect training dynamics and comparisons to natural distributions.
Quality of auxiliary training data: the CoNLL subset was annotated by a single author with no IAA reported; its contribution to ensemble gains is therefore uncertain due to possible label bias.

Cross-dataset transfer causes: declines in cross-dataset accuracy are observed, but it is unclear how much is due to annotation-guideline differences, genre (BNC vs Wikipedia), parser divergences, or sampling bias.
model_diversity_effects: Ensembles combining models trained on different corpora and configurations produce modest performance improvements, suggesting complementary information in dataset or configuration diversity (e.g., different embedding dims, paragraph vs PreWin inputs, and CoNLL-augmented training).

However, ensemble gains appear partly confounded with additional annotated data (CoNLL subset); reviewers flagged that model diversity and extra-data effects need decomposition (i.e., the incremental benefit of diversity vs the benefit of more labels).

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The paper presents Predicate Window (PreWin), a dependency-head-guided local context extractor combined with a compact LSTM-based classifier, and introduces ReLocaR, a balanced Wikipedia-derived dataset for location metonymy resolution. Reported experiments show PreWin single models outperform immediate fixed-window and paragraph baselines on both SemEval 2007 (location subset) and ReLocaR; small ensembles (including a CoNLL-annotated auxiliary set) give modest additional gains that numerically match/very slightly exceed a previously reported SemEval number. The authors emphasize a low-resource pipeline (SpaCy + GloVe + small LSTMs) and document ReLocaR annotation guidelines (notably treating governmental/political senses as metonymic) with IAA reported for test slices. Reviewers agree the idea is linguistically motivated and practically promising but identify important gaps in reproducibility, ablations, statistical reporting, parser sensitivity, and dataset sampling/annotation transparency that limit the strength and generality of some claims.
strengths: Clear, linguistically-motivated design: PreWin operationalises following the entity's dependency head to capture a compact predicate-centred window, which is conceptually plausible and explainable.

Resource-efficiency: the pipeline relies on modest external resources (SpaCy parsing, GloVe embeddings, small LSTMs) and shows competitive performance versus heavier prior systems in the reported setup.
Empirical consistency across two datasets: PreWin single-model results consistently outperform immediate-window and paragraph baselines on SemEval and the new ReLocaR dataset.
Dataset contribution: ReLocaR addresses class imbalance in prior benchmarks and documents annotation guideline choices (government-as-metonymic) with IAA reported for test partition subsets.
limitations: Statistical robustness under-specified: reported point estimates lack repeated-run statistics (mean±std across seeds), detailed statistical-test descriptions (test type, p-values), and therefore the marginal SemEval SOTA parity (ensemble 86.3 vs prior 86.2) cannot be confidently interpreted.

Critical ablations missing: the manuscript does not provide controlled experiments isolating key design choices (include vs exclude entity token; systematic PreWin window-size sweep; dependency-label ablation; padding/mask strategy), leaving causal attribution of gains to PreWin uncertain.

Parser-sensitivity untested: PreWin depends on dependency-head selection (SpaCy used) but no quantitative experiments compare alternative parsers or measure how parser errors affect extraction and downstream accuracy.

Dataset sampling and auxiliary annotation transparency gaps: ReLocaR's balancing step (discarding excess literal examples) is under-described, and the CoNLL auxiliary subset was single-annotator labeled without reported IAA — both raise sampling/label-bias risks that could affect training and ensemble outcomes.
open_questions: Please provide multi-seed (recommended N≥5) runs for primary experiments (single-model PreWin and baselines) with mean±std for accuracy and per-class F1, and state the exact statistical tests used (e.g., paired bootstrap, McNemar) including p-values and any multiple-comparison correction.

Can the authors present ablation results for (a) including vs excluding the entity token, (b) PreWin window sizes (systematic sweep, e.g., 1..8 or until sentence boundary), and (c) padding strategies (zero vs learned mask) to demonstrate the sensitivity of performance to these choices?

What is the effect of parser choice? Please re-run extraction/classification with at least one alternative dependency parser (e.g., Stanford/Stanza/UDPipe), report how often PreWin extractions differ, and quantify downstream performance differences and error attribution to parser mismatches.

For ReLocaR and the CoNLL subset: provide the exact sampling script/seed, the list of discarded literal examples or selection criteria used to balance classes, the full annotation files and adjudication logs, and IAA estimates (or spot-check IAA) for the training partitions and the CoNLL auxiliary subset.
consensus_snapshot: PreWin is a coherent, linguistically motivated extractor that gives compact, predicate-oriented context and empirically beats immediate fixed-window and paragraph baselines on the datasets and pipeline reported.
ReLocaR is a meaningful dataset contribution addressing class imbalance and explicitly documents a guideline change (government→metonymic) with high IAA reported for annotated test slices.

The pipeline achieves comparable numerical performance to prior resource-heavy systems in the reported configuration, but the SemEval ensemble parity is marginal and acknowledged by the authors as not significant at conventional thresholds without fuller statistical reporting.
Key transparency and robustness gaps (multi-run variance, ablations, parser-sensitivity, sampling/annotation logs, CoNLL IAA) are the main uncertainties reviewers want addressed.
disagreement_snapshot: Novelty: reviewers differ on whether PreWin is an incremental adaptation of dependency-path ideas or a noteworthy operational innovation because the exact combination (head-directed small window + entity exclusion + compact LSTM) appears uncommon in MR literature.

Severity of CoNLL single-annotator issue: some reviewers consider it a major methodological flaw that undermines ensemble claims until IAA is provided, while others view it as a manageable caveat if a spot-check IAA is released.

Interpretation of ensemble SOTA parity: reviewers debate whether the tiny numerical advantage (0.1%) is meaningful given auxiliary data and lack of variance reporting; some treat it as not substantively persuasive, others accept it as tentative evidence of potential when combined with PreWin.
uncertainty_snapshot: Magnitude and robustness of reported gains due to missing multi-seed statistics and unspecified testing procedures.

Causal contribution of the PreWin extractor versus confounding factors (parser tokenisation/parsing choices, dataset balancing, extra annotated data used in ensembles) because key ablations and controlled comparisons are absent.
Generalisability across parsers/genres and to natural (unbalanced) distributions because parser sensitivity and sampling-bias effects are unquantified.
Reliability of auxiliary-data-driven ensemble improvements given CoNLL subset annotation lacks independent validation (IAA).

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper proposes Predicate Window (PreWin), a dependency-head-guided extractor paired with a small LSTM model, and introduces ReLocaR, a balanced Wikipedia-derived dataset with a documented guideline shift (government/political senses labelled metonymic). Experiments show PreWin outperforms immediate-window and paragraph baselines on SemEval and ReLocaR; ensembles give modest extra gains that numerically match a prior reported SemEval number.
Strengths: The proposal is linguistically motivated, resource-efficient, empirically consistent across two datasets, and includes a useful dataset contribution (ReLocaR) with test-partition IAA reported.
Limitations: Main concerns are (1) lack of multi-seed statistics and fully described statistical tests making marginal SOTA parity hard to interpret; (2) missing ablations for entity-token exclusion, window-size choices, and padding strategies, leaving causal attribution to PreWin uncertain; (3) parser-sensitivity is unquantified though PreWin relies on correct dependency-head selection; (4) dataset-sampling transparency and single-annotator CoNLL auxiliary data lack IAA, creating potential sampling/label-bias confounds.
Open Questions: Please provide (a) multi-seed mean±std and exact statistical tests for reported contrasts, (b) ablation results for entity inclusion and window-size sweep (1..8+), (c) parser-sensitivity experiments with at least one alternate dependency parser and quantitative error attribution, and (d) full ReLocaR sampling scripts, discarded-instance lists, annotation/adjudication logs, and IAA or spot re-annotation for the CoNLL subset.
Transparency: The manuscript currently names SpaCy and GloVe and reports high-level architecture and dataset numbers, but lacks reproducibility artifacts (code, exact dependency versions, hyperparameter lists, seeds, dataset release and sampling scripts, ensemble mechanics). Reviewers recommend publishing a reproducibility bundle and running the additional analyses above to substantiate and clarify the claims. Absent these, the core engineering idea (dependency-head predicate window) is plausible and empirically promising on the authors' pipeline but its generality and the robustness of marginal SOTA claims remain uncertain.

confidence_interval.rationale: Given the consistent reported improvements of PreWin over immediate/paragraph baselines across two datasets and reviewers' agreement on the method's conceptual plausibility, there is moderate confidence the approach yields empirical benefits in the reported pipeline. However, missing multi-run statistics, ablations, parser-sensitivity tests, and dataset/annotation transparency leave substantial uncertainty about the magnitude, causal source, and generalisability of the gains; the interval reflects this mixture of supporting evidence and important unresolved verification steps.

Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Content: eview earlier and ask more experienced people in your network for feedback. Some ACs may also offer feedback for reviews that come in good time. Irresponsible reviewers and chairs. Unfortunately, with the growing number of conference submissions, there have been more and more cases where reviewers or chairs sign up for service and then simply disappear without a warning, are late without a warning, or submit (meta-)reviews that are completely unacceptable in their quality (e.g. extremely terse, unprofessional in tone, LLM-generated). Starting in October 2024, ARR provided the authors with the opportunity to report common issues with reviews (e.g. rude reviews, ‘not novel’ criticism without providing references, etc.) The ACs will see such reports, if any, judge their merit, and take them into account when writing the meta-review. A similar functionality has now been developed for meta-reviews, with author issue reports viewable for senior area chairs. Since the reviewer and AC guidelines may also seen by the authors during the response period, some sections of these guidelines now have codes for (meta-)review issues (I1-I12) that can be reported by the authors. More details here and here. Starting in May 2025, ARR also adopts the new policy on the ‘highly irresponsible’ (meta-)reviewers. The program chairs and ARR EiCs will consider the egregious cases reported by chairs (on their own judgement or based on author reports), including the cases of extremely terse reviews, unprofessional tone, and LLM-generated reviews.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Content: eview earlier and ask more experienced people in your network for feedback. Some ACs may also offer feedback for reviews that come in good time. Irresponsible reviewers and chairs. Unfortunately, with the growing number of conference submissions, there have been more and more cases where reviewers or chairs sign up for service and then simply disappear without a warning, are late without a warning, or submit (meta-)reviews that are completely unacceptable in their quality (e.g. extremely terse, unprofessional in tone, LLM-generated). Starting in October 2024, ARR provided the authors with the opportunity to report common issues with reviews (e.g. rude reviews, ‘not novel’ criticism without providing references, etc.) The ACs will see such reports, if any, judge their merit, and take them into account when writing the meta-review. A similar functionality has now been developed for meta-reviews, with author issue reports viewable for senior area chairs. Since the reviewer and AC guidelines may also seen by the authors during the response period, some sections of these guidelines now have codes for (meta-)review issues (I1-I12) that can be reported by the authors. More details here and here. Starting in May 2025, ARR also adopts the new policy on the ‘highly irresponsible’ (meta-)reviewers. The program chairs and ARR EiCs will consider the egregious cases reported by chairs (on their own judgement or based on author reports), including the cases of extremely terse reviews, unprofessional tone, and LLM-generated reviews.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
